# The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

## Introduction

The ARMA model combines the ideas of autoregressive (AR) and moving average (MA) processes.

It is one of the most important classes of stationary time series models and forms the foundation of the Box-Jenkins methodology.

An ARMA model can capture both:

- persistence through past observations,
- short-term dependence through past shocks.

## Definition

An ARMA(\(p,q\)) process is defined by

$$
Y_t
=
\phi_1Y_{t-1}
+\phi_2Y_{t-2}
+\cdots
+\phi_pY_{t-p}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}
+\theta_2\varepsilon_{t-2}
+\cdots
+\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q},
$$

where

$$
\{\varepsilon_t\}
\sim
WN(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Here:

- \(p\) = autoregressive order,
- \(q\) = moving average order.

## Special Cases

### AR Model

If

$$
q=0,
$$

then

$$
ARMA(p,0)=AR(p).
$$

### MA Model

If

$$
p=0,
$$

then

$$
ARMA(0,q)=MA(q).
$$

Thus AR and MA processes are special cases of the ARMA model.

## The ARMA(1,1) Model

The simplest ARMA model is

$$
Y_t
=
\phi Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
$$

This model combines:

- the dependence structure of AR(1),
- the shock structure of MA(1).

## Stationarity

For ARMA processes, stationarity depends on the AR part.

For ARMA(1,1),

$$
|\phi|<1
$$

is required for stationarity.

### Examples

| \(\phi\) | Stationary? |
|-----------|-----------|
| 0.3 | Yes |
| 0.8 | Yes |
| -0.5 | Yes |
| 1.0 | No |
| 1.1 | No |

## Invertibility

Invertibility depends on the MA part.

For ARMA(1,1),

$$
|\theta|<1
$$

is required for invertibility.

This ensures a unique representation of the process.

## Mean

For a stationary ARMA(1,1),

$$
E(Y_t)=0.
$$

More generally, if a constant term is included, the mean is constant over time.

## Simulation of ARMA(1,1)

Consider

$$
Y_t
=
0.7Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
0.4\varepsilon_{t-1}.
$$


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(123)

arma11 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7, ma=.4),
  n=300
)

plot.ts(
  arma11,
  main="ARMA(1,1) Process",
  ylab=expression(Y[t])
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-arma_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Observe the persistence created by the AR component and the short-term effects created by the MA component.

## ACF of an ARMA Process


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acf(
  arma11,
  main="ACF of ARMA(1,1)"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-arma_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Unlike MA models, the ACF does not cut off.

Unlike pure AR models, the pattern is often more complex.

The ACF generally tails off toward zero.

## PACF of an ARMA Process


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacf(
  arma11,
  main="PACF of ARMA(1,1)"
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-arma_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The PACF also tails off.

This is one of the identifying characteristics of ARMA models.

## Model Identification

### AR(p)

- ACF tails off.
- PACF cuts off.

### MA(q)

- ACF cuts off.
- PACF tails off.

### ARMA(p,q)

- ACF tails off.
- PACF tails off.

Therefore ARMA models are usually identified by examining both functions simultaneously.

## Comparing AR(1), MA(1), and ARMA(1,1)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow=c(3,2))

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7),
  n=300
)

acf(ar1, main="AR(1): ACF")
pacf(ar1, main="AR(1): PACF")

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.7),
  n=300
)

acf(ma1, main="MA(1): ACF")
pacf(ma1, main="MA(1): PACF")

arma11 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7, ma=.4),
  n=300
)

acf(arma11, main="ARMA(1,1): ACF")
pacf(arma11, main="ARMA(1,1): PACF")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-arma_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Compare the characteristic patterns.

## Lag Plot

A lag plot may be used to visualize dependence.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(
  x = arma11[-length(arma11)],
  y = arma11[-1],
  xlab = expression(Y[t-1]),
  ylab = expression(Y[t]),
  pch = 16
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-arma_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The relationship is generally stronger than white noise and reflects both AR and MA effects.

## Model Estimation

An ARMA(1,1) model may be estimated using maximum likelihood.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- arima(
  arma11,
  order=c(1,0,1)
)

fit
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
arima(x = arma11, order = c(1, 0, 1))

Coefficients:
         ar1     ma1  intercept
      0.6933  0.3851    -0.0051
s.e.  0.0509  0.0733     0.2623

sigma^2 estimated as 1.029:  log likelihood = -430.61,  aic = 869.22
```


:::
:::


The estimated coefficients should be close to the values used in simulation.

## Model Selection Using AIC

Different ARMA models can be compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit1 <- arima(arma11, order=c(1,0,0))
fit2 <- arima(arma11, order=c(0,0,1))
fit3 <- arima(arma11, order=c(1,0,1))

AIC(fit1, fit2, fit3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     df      AIC
fit1  3 890.8641
fit2  3 976.2085
fit3  4 869.2151
```


:::
:::


The model with the smallest AIC is usually preferred.

## Forecasting

Forecasts are based on:

- past observations,
- estimated model parameters.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(forecast)

fit <- Arima(
  arma11,
  order=c(1,0,1)
)

forecast(fit, h=10)
```

## Summary

An ARMA(\(p,q\)) model combines:

- autoregressive dependence,
- moving average dependence.

For ARMA(1,1),

$$
Y_t
=
\phi Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
$$

Important properties:

- Stationarity depends on the AR component.
- Invertibility depends on the MA component.
- ACF tails off.
- PACF tails off.
- Widely used for stationary time series.

ARMA models provide a flexible framework for describing many real-world time series.

## Exercises

1. Simulate an ARMA(1,1) process with \(\phi=0.7\) and \(\theta=0.4\).
2. Plot the series.
3. Compute and interpret the ACF.
4. Compute and interpret the PACF.
5. Estimate an ARMA(1,1) model using `arima()`.
6. Compare AR(1), MA(1), and ARMA(1,1) using ACF and PACF plots.
7. Use AIC to compare competing models.
8. Produce 10-step-ahead forecasts and interpret the results.
